title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context. The previous page shows that for a prime P = 8m+1, −1 is a biquadratic residue. So there are b, p with P | b⁴+p⁴, and therefore P divides a number of the form x²+2y² and one of the form x²−2y² (§85 Scholion). Hence ±2 are quadratic residues mod P. Combined with the fact, taken as provable, that divisors of x²+2y² (gcd(x,y)=1) have the same form, every prime 8m+1 is x²+2y². Euler says he has now proved this Fermat theorem for the first time.

This page. Euler turns to Fermat's companion claim: every prime 8m+3 is x²+2y². He says it cannot be reached by the biquadratic-residue route. Instead he inserts a proof 'communicated to me by a friend' of the following theorem (§'85', in fact §86).

Theorem. If gcd(p,q)=1, then 2p²−q² has no divisor ≡ ±3 (mod 8).

Proof, in modern terms.
(i) Residues mod 8:
- p, q both odd: 2p²−q² ≡ 1.
- p even, q odd: 2p²−q² ≡ −1.
- p odd, q = 2r: 2p²−q² = 2(p²−2r²), with p²−2r² ≡ ±1.
The identity p²−2r² = 2(p+r)²−(p+2r)² puts the odd half back into the form 2P²−Q², and gcd(p+r, p+2r)=1. So after removing a factor 2, every primitive value is ≡ ±1 mod 8.
(ii) Descent. Suppose d ≡ ±3 (mod 8) divides N = 2p²−q². Reduce p, q mod d to absolute values ≤ d/2; d still divides the new value. Then |N| ≤ d²/2, so the cofactor N/d is smaller than d. Since N ≡ ±1 (mod 8) up to a factor 2, the cofactor is ≡ ±3 (mod 8), so it has a prime factor ≡ ±3. That smaller number again divides a primitive 2p²−q², and p, q never become 0.
(iii) Infinite descent ends at the smallest candidates, 3 or 5. Neither can divide a primitive 2p²−q², because 2 is not a square mod 3 or mod 5.

This proves the second supplement to quadratic reciprocity in its negative half: (2/P) = −1 for P ≡ ±3 (mod 8). The next page then concludes:
- §87: +2 is a non-residue for such primes.
- §88: for P = 8m+3, −1 is also a non-residue, so −2 is a residue; with the divisor theorem for x²+2y², P = x²+2y² (Fermat).
- §89: for 8m−3, −1 is a residue, so −2 is a non-residue.
errors: Section numbering: the Theorem is numbered '85' although the Scholion just before it is also §85, and the next corollary is §87. It should be §86. This is a printing/numbering slip in the original.

Gap: reducing p, q mod d may introduce a common factor g. This needs a remark: any such g is coprime to d, because a common prime of d and g would divide the original p and q. So g² can be divided out without losing divisibility by d. Euler simply asserts that p and q 'always remain coprime'.
Gap: the sign of 2p²−q² (it can be negative) and the passage from 'cofactor ≡ ±3 mod 8' to 'has a (prime) divisor ≡ ±3 mod 8' are handled implicitly.
The descent's endpoint 'per se perspicuum' (3 and 5 cannot divide a primitive 2p²−q²) rests on 2 being a non-residue mod 3 and mod 5. This is trivial but unstated.
The whole 8m+1 and 8m+3 → x²+2y² argument depends on the divisor theorem for x²+2y². Here it is only cited as demonstrable ('demonstrari possit'), proved elsewhere by Euler.

ideas.what: Primes p ≡ 1 mod 8 are x²+2y², via −1 being a biquadratic residue (hence ±2 quadratic residues) plus the divisor theorem for x²+2y²
ideas.modern_name: Fermat's theorem on p = x²+2y²; supplementary law (2/p)=1 for p ≡ 1 mod 8
ideas.usually_credited_to: Stated by Fermat; first proofs by Euler (this paper, 1772/1774) and Lagrange (Recherches d'arithmétique, 1773–75)
ideas.where_published: E449 itself (Novi Comm. Petrop. 18); discussed in Weil, Number Theory: An Approach through History

ideas.what: No divisor ≡ ±3 mod 8 of primitive 2p²−q², proved by mod-8 analysis, the identity p²−2r² = 2(p+r)²−(p+2r)², and infinite descent
ideas.modern_name: Second supplementary law of quadratic reciprocity, (2/p) = −1 for p ≡ ±3 mod 8, proved by Fermat-style descent
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (via an unnamed friend) and Lagrange 1775; the full supplementary law later by Gauss (Disquisitiones, 1801)
ideas.where_published: E449 (proof attributed by Euler to an unnamed 'amicus'; identity of the friend: unsure)

ideas.what: Identity p²−2r² = 2(p+r)²−(p+2r)², mapping values of x²−2y² to values of 2x²−y²
ideas.modern_name: Equivalence of forms x²−2y² and −(y²−2x²) via a unimodular substitution, related to the unit 1+√2 in Z[√2]
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical; implicit in Euler and Lagrange's reduction theory of binary quadratic forms
ideas.where_published: E449; similar manipulations throughout Euler's work on Pell-type forms

ideas.what: For p ≡ 3 mod 8: −1 and 2 are both non-residues, so −2 is a residue, giving p = x²+2y² (next page)
ideas.modern_name: Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol; representation by x²+2y²
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler / Lagrange; Gauss for the systematic theory

deep.surprise_reason: Well-known material. These are the standard Euler/Lagrange-era proofs of the x²+2y² theorems and the negative half of the second supplementary law, documented in Weil's history. The only open historical point is the identity of the 'amicus', on which I am unsure. That is a minor attribution question, not a missed mathematical result.
transcription_corrections: No substantive errors found against the image; the duplicated section number '85' for the Theorem is in the original print, not a transcription slip.
